claim: RFC 2697 (srTCM) meters traffic with two token buckets C and E, of sizes CBS and EBS, both filled at rate CIR.
quote: The behavior of the Meter is specified in terms of its mode and two token buckets, C and E, which both share the common rate CIR. The maximum size of the token bucket C is CBS
source: RFC 2697, A Single Rate Three Color Marker (Heinanen, Guerin; Informational)

claim: In RFC 2697 tokens are added CIR times per second, filling bucket C up to CBS before E.
quote: Thereafter, the token counts Tc and Te are updated CIR times per second as follows: o If Tc is less than CBS, Tc is incremented by one, else
source: RFC 2697, A Single Rate Three Color Marker

claim: The Linux Token Bucket Filter starts full, refills tokens at a steady rate until full, and queues packets when no tokens are left.
quote: On creation, the TBF is stocked with tokens which correspond to the amount of traffic that can be burst in one go. Tokens arrive at a steady rate, until the bucket is full.
source: Linux man page tc-tbf(8)
note: Next sentence: 'If no tokens are available, packets are queued, up to a configured limit.'

claim: TBF is a pure shaper that may throttle itself so the configured rate is never exceeded.
quote: TBF is a pure shaper and never schedules traffic. It is non-work- conserving and may throttle itself, although packets are available, to ensure that the configured rate is not exceeded.
source: Linux man page tc-tbf(8)
note: 'non-work- conserving' is a line-break hyphenation in the man page.

claim: GCRA is defined by the ATM Forum UNI and ITU-T I.371 in two equivalent forms: virtual scheduling and a continuous-state leaky bucket.
quote: Both sources describe the GCRA in two equivalent ways: as a virtual scheduling algorithm and as a continuous state leaky bucket algorithm (figure 1).
source: Wikipedia, Generic cell rate algorithm
note: Secondary source (Wikipedia); primary ITU-T I.371 not fetched. Wikipedia also says GCRA 'should be considered as a version of the leaky bucket as a meter rather than the leaky bucket as a queue'.

claim: Goodput is the part of throughput served without errors and fast enough to be useful.
quote: Goodput is the subset of the throughput that is handled without errors and with low enough latency for the client to make use of the response.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026' (republication date); no author name appears on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: Load shedding keeps goodput steady as offered load rises beyond capacity.
quote: If load shedding is working, goodput will remain steady even as offered throughput increases well beyond the scaled capabilities of the service.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026' (republication date); no author name appears on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: Lower layers like iptables can reject excess connections far more cheaply than the server process.
quote: The iptables utility can put an upper bound on the number of connections that the server will accept, and can reject excess connections far more cheaply than any server process.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026' (republication date); no author name appears on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: An overloaded server can triage requests to decide which to accept and which to turn away.
quote: Prioritizing requests When a server is overloaded, it has an opportunity to triage incoming requests to decide which ones to accept and which ones to turn away.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026' (republication date); no author name appears on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here). 'Prioritizing requests' is a section heading.

claim: A server that notices the client has timed out can skip the rest of the work.
quote: If a service has gotten partway through serving a request and notices that the client has timed out, it can skip doing the rest of the work and fail the request at that point.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026' (republication date); no author name appears on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: Liveness checks test basic connectivity and that the server process is present.
quote: Liveness checks test the basic connectivity to a service and the presence of a server process.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Implementing health checks (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/implementing-health-checks/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026'; no author name on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: Local health checks go further to verify the application is likely able to function.
quote: Local health checks go further than liveness checks to verify that the application is likely to be able to function.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Implementing health checks (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/implementing-health-checks/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026'; no author name on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here).

claim: Dependency health checks inspect the application's ability to interact with adjacent systems and must be reacted to carefully because of false positives.
quote: Dependency health checks are a thorough inspection of the ability of an application to interact with its adjacent systems.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Implementing health checks (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/implementing-health-checks/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026'; no author name on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here). Also: 'Because of those false positives, we must be careful about how we react to dependency health check failures.'

claim: When all servers fail health checks at once, the load balancer fails open and sends traffic to all of them.
quote: But when all servers fail health checks at the same time, the load balancer fails open, allowing traffic to all servers.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Implementing health checks (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/implementing-health-checks/. Page shows 'Published Jun 12, 2026'; no author name on the fetched page (originally by David Yanacek, not confirmed here). Also: 'the AWS Network Load Balancer fails open if no servers are reporting as healthy.'

claim: The one-box stage deploys the latest code to the smallest deployment unit first.
quote: The one-box stage in gamma deploys the latest code to the smallest unit of deployment, such as to a single virtual machine or single container, or to a small percentage of AWS Lambda function invocations.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Clare Liguori, Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments/. Page shows author Clare Liguori, 'Published Jun 12, 2026, Last modified Jul 7, 2026' (republication).

claim: Amazon groups production deployments into waves of increasing size.
quote: We have found that grouping deployments into “waves” of increasing size, as seen in the previous sample prod pipeline, helps us achieve a good balance between deployment risk and speed.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Clare Liguori, Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments/. Page shows author Clare Liguori, 'Published Jun 12, 2026, Last modified Jul 7, 2026' (republication).

claim: A typical pipeline bakes at least one hour after each one-box stage and at least 12 hours after the first regional wave.
quote: A typical pipeline waits at least one hour after each one-box stage, at least 12 hours after the first regional wave, and at least two to four hours after each of the rest of the regional waves,
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Clare Liguori, Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments/. Page shows author Clare Liguori, 'Published Jun 12, 2026, Last modified Jul 7, 2026' (republication). Default bake times deploy a change to all Regions in about four or five business days.

claim: A high-severity alarm both pages the on-call engineer and automatically rolls back an in-progress deployment.
quote: This high-severity alarm is used to page the oncall engineer and to automatically roll back the service if a deployment is in progress.
source: Amazon Builders' Library, Clare Liguori, Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builder Center)
note: Redirected from aws.amazon.com/builders-library/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments/. Page shows author Clare Liguori, 'Published Jun 12, 2026, Last modified Jul 7, 2026' (republication).

claim: Kubernetes probe defaults: initialDelaySeconds 0 and periodSeconds 10.
quote: Defaults to 0 seconds. Minimum value is 0. periodSeconds How often (in seconds) to perform the probe. Default to 10 seconds. The minimum value is 1.
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)
note: Field-defaults list was found on this concepts page, not on the tasks page configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/ (fetched, no defaults list).

claim: Kubernetes probe timeoutSeconds defaults to 1 second.
quote: timeoutSeconds Number of seconds after which the probe times out. Defaults to 1 second. Minimum value is 1.
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)

claim: Kubernetes probe successThreshold defaults to 1 and must be 1 for liveness and startup probes.
quote: Defaults to 1. Must be 1 for liveness and startup Probes. Minimum value is 1.
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)
note: These sentences follow the successThreshold field description.

claim: Kubernetes probe failureThreshold defaults to 3 consecutive failures.
quote: failureThreshold After a probe fails failureThreshold times in a row, Kubernetes considers that the overall check has failed: the container is not ready/healthy/live. Defaults to 3.
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)

claim: Kubernetes warns that badly implemented liveness probes can cause cascading failures.
quote: Incorrect implementation of liveness probes can lead to cascading failures. This results in restarting of container under high load;
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)

claim: Kubernetes advises the liveness probe check only the app itself, while the readiness probe also checks required back-end services.
quote: The liveness probe passes when the app itself is healthy, but the readiness probe additionally checks that each required back-end service is available.
source: Kubernetes docs, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (concepts)

claim: One way to handle overload is to serve degraded responses that are cheaper to compute.
quote: One option for handling overload is to serve degraded responses: responses that are not as accurate as or that contain less data than normal responses, but that are easier to compute.
source: Google SRE book ch. 21, Handling Overload (Alejandro Forero Cuervo)
note: Date is the book's 2016 publication; page itself undated.

claim: CRITICAL_PLUS is reserved for the most critical requests.
quote: CRITICAL_PLUS Reserved for the most critical requests, those that will result in serious user-visible impact if they fail.
source: Google SRE book ch. 21, Handling Overload (Alejandro Forero Cuervo)
note: Order of the four values: CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE.

claim: Services must provision capacity for all expected CRITICAL and CRITICAL_PLUS traffic.
quote: Services are expected to provision enough capacity for all expected CRITICAL and CRITICAL_PLUS traffic.
source: Google SRE book ch. 21, Handling Overload (Alejandro Forero Cuervo)

claim: SHEDDABLE_PLUS traffic expects partial unavailability; SHEDDABLE expects frequent partial and occasional full unavailability.
quote: SHEDDABLE Traffic for which frequent partial unavailability and occasional full unavailability is expected.
source: Google SRE book ch. 21, Handling Overload (Alejandro Forero Cuervo)
note: SHEDDABLE_PLUS: 'Traffic for which partial unavailability is expected. This is the default for batch jobs, which can retry requests minutes or even hours later.'

claim: Graceful degradation goes beyond load shedding by reducing the work per request, e.g. lower-quality responses.
quote: Graceful degradation takes the concept of load shedding one step further by reducing the amount of work that needs to be performed.
source: Google SRE book ch. 22, Addressing Cascading Failures (Mike Ulrich)

claim: Graceful degradation should rarely trigger, so it must be exercised regularly to keep it working.
quote: You can make sure that graceful degradation stays working by regularly running a small subset of servers near overload in order to exercise this code path.
source: Google SRE book ch. 22, Addressing Cascading Failures (Mike Ulrich)

claim: SRE book ch. 22 uses 'graceful degradation' rather than the term brownout.
source: Google SRE book ch. 22, Addressing Cascading Failures (Mike Ulrich)
note: No occurrence of 'brownout' in ch. 22 text; the Amazon load shedding article uses 'brownout' (e.g. 'When there is a brownout, our priority is to add capacity').

claim: A 5% canary serving 20% errors gives a 1% overall error rate, so canary size bounds error budget spend.
quote: If we instead use a canary population of 5%, we serve 20% errors for 5% of traffic, resulting in a 1% overall error rate
source: Google SRE workbook ch. 16, Canarying Releases
note: Date is workbook publication year; page undated.

claim: Canary duration must fit deployment velocity: shorter for continuous deploys.
quote: If you deploy continuously (for example, 20 times in a day), your canary duration must be significantly shorter.
source: Google SRE workbook ch. 16, Canarying Releases

claim: A canary should be large and long enough to be representative.
quote: Size and duration It should be sizeable and last long enough to be representative of the overall deployment.
source: Google SRE workbook ch. 16, Canarying Releases

claim: Google strongly advises running only one canary at a time.
quote: We strongly advise running only one canary deployment at a time.
source: Google SRE workbook ch. 16, Canarying Releases

claim: Release toggles ship incomplete code to production as latent code.
quote: Release Toggles allow incomplete and un-tested codepaths to be shipped to production as latent code which may never be turned on.
source: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags), martinfowler.com
note: Categories: Release, Experiment, Ops, Permissioning Toggles. Article also dated 08 February 2016 (first publication); 09 October 2017 is the latest revision date shown.

claim: Experiment toggles drive A/B and multivariate tests.
quote: Experiment Toggles are used to perform multivariate or A/B testing.
source: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags), martinfowler.com

claim: Ops toggles let operators disable or degrade a feature quickly in production.
quote: We might introduce an Ops Toggle when rolling out a new feature which has unclear performance implications so that system operators can disable or degrade that feature quickly in production if needed.
source: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags), martinfowler.com

claim: Some long-lived ops toggles are kill switches for graceful degradation under high load.
quote: it's not uncommon for systems to have a small number of long-lived “Kill Switches” which allow operators of production environments to gracefully degrade non-vital system functionality when the system is enduring unusually high load.
source: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags), martinfowler.com

claim: Permissioning toggles change the features certain users receive.
quote: These flags are used to change the features or product experience that certain users receive.
source: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags), martinfowler.com
note: Sentence under the Permissioning Toggles heading.

claim: The bulkhead pattern isolates application elements into pools so one failure does not take down the rest.
quote: Isolate the elements of an application into pools so that if one element fails, the others continue to function.
source: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Bulkhead pattern
note: Also: 'This pattern is named after the sectioned partitions (bulkheads) of a ship's hull.'

claim: Azure describes a circuit breaker as a proxy that tracks recent failures to decide whether to allow an operation or fail immediately.
quote: The proxy should monitor the number of recent failures and use this information to decide whether to allow the operation to proceed or to return an exception immediately.
source: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Circuit Breaker pattern

claim: Netflix computes concurrency with Little's law: concurrency equals average service time times average service rate.
quote: A system’s concurrency is normally calculated using Little’s law, which states: For a system at steady state, concurrency is the product of the average service time and the average service rate (L = 𝛌W).
source: Netflix Technology Blog, Eran Landau, William Thurston, Tim Bozarth, Performance Under Load (Adaptive Concurrency Limits @ Netflix)
note: Live URLs netflixtechblog.com/performance-under-load-3e6fa9a60581 and medium.com returned 403/Cloudflare block; quote taken from the Wayback Machine copy.

claim: Netflix's gradient algorithm scales the limit by RTTnoload/RTTactual and adds an allowed queue size.
quote: This ratio gives us the gradient or magnitude of latency change: gradient=(RTTnoload/RTTactual) . A value of 1 indicates no queueing and that the limit can be increased.
source: Netflix Technology Blog, Eran Landau, William Thurston, Tim Bozarth, Performance Under Load (Adaptive Concurrency Limits @ Netflix)
note: Live URLs netflixtechblog.com/performance-under-load-3e6fa9a60581 and medium.com returned 403/Cloudflare block; quote taken from the Wayback Machine copy.

claim: Each sample updates the limit as currentLimit times gradient plus an allowed queue size.
quote: With each new sample the limit adjusts using this ratio and adding an allowable queue size using the simple formula, newLimit = currentLimit × gradient + queueSize
source: Netflix Technology Blog, Eran Landau, William Thurston, Tim Bozarth, Performance Under Load (Adaptive Concurrency Limits @ Netflix)
note: Live URLs netflixtechblog.com/performance-under-load-3e6fa9a60581 and medium.com returned 403/Cloudflare block; quote taken from the Wayback Machine copy.

claim: The concurrency-limits README frames limits as concurrent requests via Little's Law, Limit = Average RPS * Average Latency.
quote: This relationship is covered very nicely with Little's Law where `Limit = Average RPS * Average Latency`.
source: Netflix/concurrency-limits README (GitHub, master)

claim: concurrency-limits borrows TCP congestion control, treating a concurrency limit like a congestion window.
quote: To estimate the limit we borrow from common TCP congestion control algorithms by equating a system's concurrency limit to a TCP congestion window.
source: Netflix/concurrency-limits README (GitHub, master)
